flashcards.q: Why is multi-column PDF text extraction a 'silent' failure?
flashcards.a: Text extraction that ignores layout reads content in the PDF's internal object order, which for two columns is often interleaved line-by-line across columns. The result is fluent, grammatically plausible but semantically scrambled text -- no exception thrown, nothing looks obviously broken.

flashcards.q: Name the three table-handling strategies and when to use each.
flashcards.a: Markdown serialization (default, small-medium tables, repeat header row). Per-row records (large tables exceeding chunk budget, header carried per row group, row index as metadata). Summary + reference (very large/wide tables where per-row produces too many near-duplicate chunks -- summarize for retrieval, keep full table as reference).

flashcards.q: Which PDF parsers have documented strengths/weaknesses on multi-column layouts?
flashcards.a: LlamaParse's 'accurate' mode has a documented reading-order weakness on multi-column layouts. Docling and Marker-PDF are more commonly recommended for documents with complex multi-column layouts (academic papers, dense reports). Validate against your own corpus rather than assuming one tool generalizes.

flashcards.q: Why must code be split on AST boundaries rather than character/line counts?
flashcards.a: Character/line splitting routinely cuts a function mid-body or discards its enclosing class/import context, producing a fragment that's frequently unusable for code generation/review. AST-aware splitting (tree-sitter) guarantees chunks are syntactically complete units except for the rare oversized-function case.

flashcards.q: What paper formalizes AST-based code chunking as a measurable retrieval-quality improvement?
flashcards.a: cAST (arXiv:2506.15655) -- shows AST-based structural chunking improves code-RAG retrieval quality over naive line-based splitting, not just as an intuitive best practice.

flashcards.q: What is parent-child hierarchical retrieval and what problem does it solve?
flashcards.a: Index small leaf chunks for precise embedding similarity search, but substitute the parent chunk at retrieval time when enough of its children are retrieved together (LlamaIndex AutoMergingRetriever). Solves the case where a document's sections vary widely in natural density -- no single flat chunk size serves both a short definition and a dense multi-page procedure well.

flashcards.q: Why is a captioned image a lossy representation, and what's the practical consequence?
flashcards.a: A caption compresses the image's full information content into text, so retrieval only succeeds for queries the caption's text actually captures. A vague caption ('a chart showing data') gives retrieval nothing to match a specific query against, even though the answer is visible in the image.

flashcards.q: What can knowledge-graph-augmented RAG do that flat chunk retrieval structurally cannot?
flashcards.a: Answer multi-hop questions requiring connections across many documents (e.g. 'which vendors does our largest customer's parent company also do business with') and 'global' whole-corpus-summary questions, since similarity search has no notion of relationship structure across entities.

flashcards.q: Give the real cost numbers for GraphRAG's original cost profile.
flashcards.a: Entity/relation extraction inflates token usage ~3-5x over plain chunking. Early indexing runs for a large corpus were reported around $33,000 (2024). Query-time graph traversal/community summarization adds a measured 2-3x higher end-to-end latency versus flat retrieval.

flashcards.q: How much has GraphRAG indexing cost dropped, and what techniques drove it?
flashcards.a: Microsoft reports indexing cost falling to roughly 0.1% of its original 2024 figure within about 18 months via better extraction prompting and caching. LightRAG cuts indexing token cost ~60% and roughly halves median query latency. KET-RAG limits expensive LLM extraction to a PageRank-selected subset of chunks combined with a cheap keyword-bipartite graph.

flashcards.q: Why do PDF headers and footers need special handling instead of being chunked as body text?
flashcards.a: Running titles, page numbers, and repeated boilerplate appear identically on nearly every page; chunking them as body content pollutes the corpus with dozens/hundreds of near-duplicate, low-information chunks competing for top-k slots against genuinely useful content.

flashcards.q: What triggers OCR fallback in a PDF ingestion pipeline, and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: Per-page text-density detection: born-digital pages extract directly via the text layer, but scanned pages have no text layer and a text-only pipeline silently returns empty/near-empty content for them. OCR (EasyOCR/Tesseract) is triggered specifically for low-text-density pages.

flashcards.q: Why is provenance metadata a first-class requirement for every structured unit produced during ingestion?
flashcards.a: Without source_id, page/section, and extraction-method metadata, a wrong answer traced to a scrambled multi-column extraction or a bad OCR read looks identical to any other retrieval failure, and the error-analysis loop (T06-accuracy-tuning) has nothing to classify against.
